summary_vn: Chào hỏi, ngủ trưa, mưa nắng, xe máy, thăm nhà — những thứ ai sống ở Việt Nam cũng quen, nhưng khó giải thích cho bạn nước ngoài bằng tiếng Anh.
summary_en: Greetings, midday naps, weather, motorbike traffic, dropping by unannounced — the daily-life rhythms a Vietnamese speaker takes for granted but has to explain again every time a non-Vietnamese friend visits.
regional_note: Cách chào, giờ ăn trưa, kiểu thời tiết khác nhau giữa Bắc và Nam — Hà Nội có mùa đông thật sự, Sài Gòn quanh năm hai mùa mưa khô. Vài cụm từ ở đây sẽ tự nhiên hơn ở miền này hoặc miền kia, đã ghi chú trong từng phrase khi cần.

phrases.vn_moment: 'Ăn cơm chưa?' — câu chào, không phải câu hỏi
phrases.context: Bạn nước ngoài nghe người Việt hỏi nhau và bối rối.
phrases.english: When older Vietnamese people say 'Have you eaten yet?' — that's a greeting, not a real question. The expected answer is just 'Yes, I have' even if you haven't. It's the way 'how are you' works in English: nobody actually wants the long version.
phrases.cultural_note: Answering with a detailed 'no, I'm starving, what do you have' lands as a request for food. The greeting form expects a closed yes-or-no, then we move on.

phrases.vn_moment: 'Đi đâu đó?' — chào nhau khi gặp ngoài đường
phrases.context: Hàng xóm bắt gặp bạn ở cổng và hỏi 'đi đâu đó?'.
phrases.english: If a Vietnamese neighbor catches you leaving the house and says 'Where are you going?' — they're not actually demanding your itinerary. It's a greeting. A vague answer like 'just running an errand' or 'out for a bit' closes the loop.
phrases.cultural_note: Detailed answers feel oversharing; refusing to answer ('why do you ask') reads as cold. The vague-but-friendly version is the cultural sweet spot.

phrases.vn_moment: Gọi người lạ bằng anh / chị / cô / chú
phrases.context: Đặt đồ ăn — gọi người bán hàng kiểu nào?
phrases.english: We address strangers using family titles based on their age relative to ours — 'anh' for a man slightly older, 'chị' for a woman, 'cô' or 'chú' for someone old enough to be a parent. It's the polite default. Calling a stranger by their name alone, or just 'you,' would feel cold.
phrases.cultural_note: English doesn't have an equivalent — 'sir' / 'ma'am' is the closest, but those land more formal than 'anh' / 'chị.' The age-based read happens in seconds and rarely gets it wrong.

phrases.vn_moment: Hỏi tuổi — chuyện thường
phrases.context: Bạn Mỹ ngạc nhiên khi đồng nghiệp hỏi 'how old are you' phút đầu gặp.
phrases.english: Asking someone's age in the first conversation is normal in Vietnamese culture — we need it to know which family title to use. It's not rudeness; it's the system. In English you can deflect with 'I'm in my thirties' if you don't want to give a number.
phrases.cultural_note: Westerners often hear age questions as personal probing. From a Vietnamese frame, it's just navigation — like asking where someone works.

phrases.vn_moment: Ngủ trưa — không phải lười
phrases.context: Văn phòng đóng cửa từ 12 đến 1:30 giờ trưa.
phrases.english: Most workplaces in Vietnam shut for an hour or more around lunch — people eat, then sleep at their desks for twenty or thirty minutes. It's not laziness; it's how we get through the afternoon heat. Trying to schedule a 12:30 meeting will feel as wrong as a 6am meeting in the West.
phrases.cultural_note: If you're scheduling with a Vietnamese counterpart, leave 12:00 to 1:30 alone. Even remote workers tend to be offline during that window.

phrases.vn_moment: Ăn sáng ngoài hàng — ai cũng làm
phrases.context: Bạn Tây ngạc nhiên vì sao buổi sáng quán phở đầy người.
phrases.english: In Vietnam, eating breakfast out is the default — phở, bún, xôi, bánh mì from a street stall on the way to work. Cooking breakfast at home is the exception, not the rule. Stalls open at 5 or 6am for the office crowd.
phrases.cultural_note: This often surprises Western visitors — 'restaurants' open before sunrise. The economics work because the stalls are family-run and small.

phrases.vn_moment: Xe máy là phương tiện chính
phrases.context: Bạn Mỹ bước qua đường lần đầu ở Hà Nội và đứng tê.
phrases.english: Motorbikes are the default transport in Vietnamese cities — there are more bikes than cars, often by ten to one. Crossing the street works by walking steadily and predictably. The bikes flow around you. Stopping or running is what causes accidents.
phrases.cultural_note: Western pedestrian instincts say 'wait for a gap.' Vietnamese streets don't have gaps. Walking calmly is the actual safe move; first-time visitors often need a local to walk with them once.

phrases.vn_moment: Bốn người trên một xe máy
phrases.context: Bạn nước ngoài chụp hình và ngạc nhiên.
phrases.english: It's normal to see a whole family on one motorbike — dad driving, mom on the back, two small kids in between. Helmets are required by law for adults. It looks impossible to outsiders; for us it's the family car.
phrases.cultural_note: Treating it as exotic photo material can land as condescending. It's the practical solution to a transport problem, not a spectacle.

phrases.vn_moment: Mùa mưa — đường ngập, đời vẫn sống
phrases.context: Đồng nghiệp Mỹ ngạc nhiên vì sao Sài Gòn ngập mà ai cũng đi làm.
phrases.english: Vietnam has two seasons in the south — rainy from May to October, dry the rest. During rainy season, streets flood for half an hour after a downpour, then drain. People still go to work. We have rain ponchos that go over the motorbike, not just the rider.
phrases.cultural_note: 'Snow days' don't exist for rain. The infrastructure assumes flooding; cancelling work over weather would feel excessive.

phrases.vn_moment: Cởi giày trước khi vào nhà
phrases.context: Bạn Tây vào nhà bạn người Việt mà không tháo giày.
phrases.english: We take shoes off before entering a Vietnamese home — there's usually a rack or a pile by the door. If the host offers slippers, use them. If they don't, socks or bare feet are fine. Tracking outside dirt onto floor people sit and eat on is the underlying reason.
phrases.cultural_note: Hosts almost never ask out loud. Watch what others did at the door, or notice the shoe pile — that's the cue. Western guests forgetting once is forgivable; doing it twice signals you weren't paying attention.

phrases.vn_moment: Ghé chơi không hẹn trước
phrases.context: Bạn Tây ngạc nhiên khi bạn người Việt nói 'tao ghé qua' không gọi điện trước.
phrases.english: In Vietnam, friends and relatives often drop by without a phone call — knocking on the gate or showing up at the door is common. The host is expected to make tea, sit a bit, and chat for ten or fifteen minutes. Rejecting an unannounced visit reads as cold.
phrases.cultural_note: This is changing in younger urban circles, who text first. But across generations, the unannounced visit is still the norm — you'll see it especially with parents and grandparents.

phrases.vn_moment: Từ chối đồ ăn dù muốn
phrases.context: Bạn nước ngoài thấy bạn người Việt từ chối khi được mời ăn.
phrases.english: When a Vietnamese host offers food the first time, the polite reflex is to decline once — 'oh, I'm fine, don't trouble yourself.' The host then offers again, and that's when you accept. Saying yes immediately can feel grasping. Saying no twice can feel rude back.
phrases.cultural_note: The two-round dance is dying out in younger generations and dying faster in cities. But with parents, grandparents, or rural relatives, expect it. Western 'just say what you want' directness reads as bluntness here.

phrases.vn_moment: Trả tiền — ai mời người đó trả
phrases.context: Bạn Mỹ rút thẻ chia tiền sau bữa cơm với gia đình bạn.
phrases.english: Splitting the bill isn't the Vietnamese default — whoever invited usually pays. If a Vietnamese friend invites you to a meal, expect them to cover it. Offering to split can feel like rejecting their hospitality. Reciprocate by inviting them next time.
phrases.cultural_note: Younger urban Vietnamese, especially in coffee-shop circles, do split bills now. Among older relatives or in formal contexts, the inviter-pays default still holds.

phrases.vn_moment: Lì xì — không chỉ ngày Tết
phrases.context: Đồng nghiệp Mỹ thấy bao đỏ ở đám cưới và hỏi.
phrases.english: Red envelopes — 'lì xì' — show up at Tết for kids, but also at weddings, birthdays for grandparents, and house-warming visits. The amount inside matters less than the gesture. New, crisp bills are the standard.
phrases.cultural_note: Old, folded bills can land as 'leftover money.' If you're invited to a Vietnamese wedding and want to give cash the local way, swap for fresh notes at the bank first.

phrases.vn_moment: Sinh nhật lịch âm hay lịch dương?
phrases.context: Đồng nghiệp Mỹ thắc mắc vì sao mỗi năm sinh nhật bạn rơi vào ngày khác.
phrases.english: Older Vietnamese people often celebrate birthdays by the lunar calendar, which means the date shifts by a couple of weeks each year on the solar calendar. Younger people use the solar date. If a relative wishes you happy birthday on a 'wrong' day, they're using the lunar one — both are correct.
phrases.cultural_note: When asking a Vietnamese friend's birthday for a calendar invite, clarify 'solar or lunar?' once and you'll save the annual confusion.

phrases.vn_moment: Tết, Giỗ tổ — nghỉ theo lịch âm
phrases.context: Quản lý Mỹ không hiểu vì sao mỗi năm Tết Việt Nam rơi vào ngày khác.
phrases.english: Vietnam's biggest holidays — Tết especially — are on the lunar calendar, so the dates move every year. Tết can land anywhere from late January to mid-February. Most companies give a full week off. If you have Vietnamese reports or partners, check the lunar date in December for the next year's planning.
phrases.cultural_note: Calling Tết 'Chinese New Year' technically gets the date right but misses the cultural specificity. 'Lunar New Year' or 'Vietnamese New Year' is more accurate.

phrases.vn_moment: Lương / vợ chồng / con — hỏi sớm là bình thường
phrases.context: Người quen mới hỏi 'lương bao nhiêu' và 'có vợ chưa' phút thứ năm.
phrases.english: Older Vietnamese strangers may ask about salary, marital status, and kids in the first ten minutes — 'are you married yet,' 'how much do you make,' 'when are kids coming.' It's not nosiness in our frame; it's how relatives and neighbors map you. A vague answer is fine: 'comfortable' for salary, 'not yet, busy with work' for marriage.
phrases.cultural_note: Younger Vietnamese, especially diaspora, have absorbed Western privacy norms and ask less directly. Older generations and rural relatives ask the same questions every visit — that's not disrespect, it's the script.

phrases.vn_moment: Nhậu — uống bia ăn mồi sau giờ làm
phrases.context: Đồng nghiệp Mỹ được mời 'đi nhậu' và không hiểu nghĩa.
phrases.english: 'Nhậu' is the after-work eating-and-drinking session — usually beer, sometimes rice wine, with small dishes shared at a sidewalk table. It's the Vietnamese equivalent of going for drinks, but slower and more food-heavy. Declining an invitation isn't insulting, but joining once is the fastest way to be welcomed onto a team.
phrases.cultural_note: 'Nhậu' is mostly a male tradition in older contexts, though that's shifting fast. Pacing yourself is fine; toasts come around ('một, hai, ba, dô!') and matching every one will end your evening early.

phrases.vn_moment: Karaoke — chuyện họp công ty
phrases.context: Sếp rủ cả đội đi karaoke sau bữa tiệc tất niên.
phrases.english: Karaoke in Vietnam isn't just a fun option — it's often where bonding actually happens after a work dinner. Rooms are private, you book by the hour, you sing whether you can or not. Refusing a song from the boss can read as standoffish. Pick something easy, get it done, then nobody asks again.
phrases.cultural_note: It's normal to be terrible. The performance isn't the point; the willingness is. Western 'I don't sing' often gets read as not wanting to participate, even when meant literally.

phrases.vn_moment: Người lớn gắp đồ ăn vào bát mình
phrases.context: Bạn Mỹ ngạc nhiên khi mẹ bạn gắp miếng cá vào bát họ.
phrases.english: If a Vietnamese host or older relative reaches over and puts food in your bowl with their chopsticks, that's affection — it means they want to make sure you eat well. Refusing reads as rejecting the care. Eat what they gave you; you don't have to finish everything else.
phrases.cultural_note: In Western etiquette this can feel like an invasion. From the Vietnamese side, it's the same impulse as a Western host offering seconds — just with motor function attached.

dialogues.title: First-time visitor crosses the street
dialogues.setting: Your American friend is visiting Hanoi and freezes at a busy intersection.

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.english: I'm not crossing this. There's no break in the bikes.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: There won't be one. Just walk slowly and don't stop. They'll go around you.

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.english: That sounds like the worst possible advice.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: I know. But the bikes are tracking you the whole time — they're watching where you're going to be in two seconds. If you suddenly stop or run, that's when you become unpredictable. Just walk.

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.english: Okay. Hold my arm.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Sure. We'll go together. Don't look at the bikes — look at the curb on the other side. Steady pace.

lines.speaker: Friend
lines.english: ...Oh. They really do go around.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Yeah. Welcome to Hanoi.

dialogues.title: Coworker is invited to dinner at your parents' house
dialogues.setting: Your American coworker is visiting your family for the first time.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: Should I bring something? Wine?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Fruit is the safe choice — a nice basket from a market. My parents don't really drink wine. And take your shoes off at the door. There's a rack.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: Got it. Anything I shouldn't do?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: When my mom offers food the first time, you'll probably say 'oh I'm fine.' She'll ask again. That's when you accept. If you say yes the first time, it can feel grabby. If you say no twice, she thinks you don't like her cooking.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: That's a tightrope.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: It's softer than it sounds. And if she puts something on your plate with her chopsticks — that's affection. Eat it. You don't have to finish everything else, but eat the thing she gave you.

lines.speaker: Coworker
lines.english: And if she asks if I'm married, when I'm having kids, what I make?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Vague answers are fine. 'Not yet, busy with work' covers most of them. She's not being nosy — that's how she's mapping you. By the third visit, the same questions will be friendlier.

dialogues.title: Manager schedules a 12:30 meeting
dialogues.setting: Your American manager wants a quick sync with your Vietnam team and proposes 12:30pm Vietnam time.

lines.speaker: Manager
lines.english: Can we get the Hanoi team on a quick call at 12:30 their time? Just twenty minutes.

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: That's the lunch and nap window — most of the team will be away from the desk between 12 and 1:30. Even the remote folks tend to be offline.

lines.speaker: Manager
lines.english: Nap window?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: Yeah, midday rest is standard there. Twenty minutes after lunch, sometimes longer. It's how people get through the afternoon heat. Trying to book that hour will feel as off as me trying to book you for a 6am call.

lines.speaker: Manager
lines.english: Got it. Push to 2pm their time?

lines.speaker: You
lines.english: 2pm works. People are back, fed, and reasonably awake. That's the sweet spot for a quick sync with the Vietnam side.
